19909-good-cheer-stories-every-child-sho:
Good Cheer Stories Every Child Should Know, dated 1915, collects tales of kindness. One opens in the country of the Greedy, ruled by a troubled king. His subjects behave well but love pies and tarts too much. Soup disgusts them as if it were sea water. A policeman could barely make them open their mouths for meat. Such appetites plainly need a story's cure.

Asa Don Dickinson edited this Hamilton Wright Mabie series volume. The Every Child Should Know books stocked home libraries nationwide. Good cheer here means generosity, gratitude, and unselfish joy. Tales from many authors teach those virtues by example. The Greedy country shows the method in miniature. It is wholesome reading, skillfully chosen.
20193-mary-s-rainbow:
Mary's Rainbow, from 1922, is a children's tale set around a sick child's care. A kindly voice praises Sister Julia and her way with children. One child, now much improved, no longer needs her daily care. So Sister Julia should go to a poor little fellow who does.

That shift of care opens a story of illness, kindness, and hope. Nuns who nursed children play a warm, central role in such tales. A rainbow, as the title hints, promises brightness after a storm. Young readers get a gentle tale of sickness healed by love and skill.
22406-the-little-people-of-the-snow:
The Little People of the Snow is a poem of winter in a mountain glen. It watches a little brook as cold weather transforms its banks. Later flowers give way to white, crystal forms of frost.

Those white flowers grow in clear November nights, the poem says. Later still, drifted snow fills the glen from side to side. A person might walk across the buried stream safely. Many fathoms deep below, the brook still runs unfrozen. It sings to itself and leaps over its pebbles. The poem finds hidden life under winter's still surface. Readers get nature verse that rewards slow, close watching.
22637-a-little-window:
A Little Window is a book of nature poems, written in a loose, singing free verse. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its title suggests a small opening on a large world, and the sample looks down a gorge at a river in autumn.

The river curls and hums its cadences, slipping past under the gorge's rim as the poet peers through scarlet sumacs. It sparkles in sunlight and shimmers in moonlight, going on and on like a silvery sheet of song. Such verse prizes mood and music over tight form. The collection belongs to the era when American poetry was loosening its meters and turning to the native landscape for its images. It offers a quiet, watery hour of reading.
23277-feats-on-the-fiord-the-third-book-:
Feats on the Fiord is the third book in the Playfellow series, set on the coast of Norway. Its waters are busy with life. Boatmen row out to check the sea-fowl on islet after islet, or carry out nets and rods for the fish that fill those waters.

Sea-trout and char, cod and herrings abound there in their seasons. Between the splash of fish and the dip of oars, the fiord is drawn as a working world, not a backdrop. Readers get children's adventure in a Norwegian fishing landscape, where skill on the water is the real feat.
aaron-trow: Trollope's Aaron Trow is a dark and powerful tale of the Bermudas. An escaped convict terrorizes a small and lonely island settlement. The tense story grips the reader like a vice. One of Trollope's grimmest short works.
and-even-now: Max Beerbohm's 1920 essays: "And Even Now" gathers his late wit on the changing world. Elegant and melancholy, they show the master in his maturity. Irony at its most refined. Beerbohm's late essays are autumnal and exquisite.
at-the-foot-of-the-rainbow: A gentle romance set among the farms and woods of rural Indiana. Gene Stratton-Porter, famous for weaving nature into her fiction, tells of two neighboring farmers whose friendship is tested by love, pride, and a tragedy in the marshes. Birds, wildflowers, and country seasons shape nearly every scene, making the landscape itself one of the book's main characters.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-our-lady-of-t: Our Lady of the Snow is the legend of the August snowfall that marked where St. Mary Major should rise. This entry explains the story, its feast, and its basilica. Snow in summer, by Mary's hand: its feast falls on August 5.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-brist: Richard Bristow was the Douai scholar of the seminary's founding. This entry notes his learning, his works, and his life. The pillar of the English college: his deep learning armed the missionary priests of England's mission in the 1500s' peril.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rose-window: The rose window is the wheel of stained glass. This entry explains its form, its symbolism, and its masters. The flower of the Gothic facade: its colored glass glows at sunset in Chartres's nave in France's heart of faith and stone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-dur: The School of Durrow was the monastery of the midland Irish. This entry covers its founder, its book, and its fame. The learning of the Offaly plain: its great book crowns the Gospels in the 600s' scriptorium of the monks.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stanislawow: Stanislawow was the diocese of Galicia. This entry traces its see, its Ruthenians, and its churches. The bishopric of the eastern border: its new see crowned Stanislawow in the 1880s' Galicia in the east of the province in the Ukraine.

doe-osti-3912522-frequency-extraction-fr: Accelerator beams wobble at characteristic frequencies — reading them reveals the machine's health. Yongjun Li's work extracts frequencies from invariant flows, the orderly patterns hidden in beam motion. The technique gives operators a sharper diagnostic for tuning their machines.
fern-s-hollow: Fern's Hollow, by Hesba Stretton. The hollow's tale. This book preserves that children's story. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. Its place in history is secure. Kept for study. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it.
flame-and-shadow: A 1920 poetry collection by Sara Teasdale, one of America's most popular lyric poets. Her short, musical verses speak of love, beauty, and sorrow with a clarity that made her work beloved by ordinary readers. Many of these poems were set to music, and the collection captures Teasdale at her peak: simple on the surface, quietly heartbreaking underneath.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Ex:
On September 15, 1970, President Richard Nixon met in the Oval Office for twenty minutes with his advisers. In that short meeting, from 3:25 to 3:45 in the afternoon, he ordered the CIA to push for a military coup in Chile. Peter Kornbluh edited this briefing book, posted fifty years later in September 2020.

The target was Salvador Allende, Chile's newly elected socialist president, before he could take office. The declassified records behind the posting trace how that order set covert action in motion. It is a compact, dated record of the moment the United States chose the most extreme option against an elected government.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Th:
Nearly half a century after General Augusto Pinochet seized power in Chile, key American records about the coup were still secret. This briefing book asks the classic question in its title: what did President Richard Nixon know, and when did he know it?

Its point is the gap itself. Presidential and CIA documents from 1973 remained withheld forty-nine years after the putsch, long after most of the main facts were public. For readers, the posting is evidence of how long intelligence files can stay locked even when the history around them is well known.
his-last-bow: His Last Bow, Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes stories. The detective's farewell. This book preserves that collection. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
lazy-thoughts-of-a-lazy-girl-sister-of-t:
Jenny Wren wrote Lazy Thoughts of a Lazy Girl as a set of light essays. Hurst and Company published it in New York. She bills herself as sister of that Idle Fellow.

Twelve short chapters treat love, bills, politics, and afternoon tea. Dress, Christmas, town, and country each get a chapter. Children, dogs, concerts, and dancing fill the later pages. Her tone is chatty, amused, and deliberately unhurried. The book offers Victorian drawing room humor in small, easy doses. Her laziness is a pose for wit, not true idleness. Each short chapter lands one or two neat social jokes.
little-sister-snow:
Frances Little published this Japan story in 1909. Genjiro Kataoka supplied the illustrations. She dedicates it to her niece Alice Hegan Rice. Happy months spent together in Japan inspired the dedication.

Its heroine, Yuki San, is called before her father early. She paints, serves tea, and promises the gods faithfully. Two old people and flying feet fill the picture list. Little, author of The Lady of the Decoration, sets childhood in Japan. Yuki busies herself serving tea in one listed illustration. Not willing to be surpassed in salutation, another caption reads.
love-s-shadow:
Love's Shadow, first published in London in 1908, opens Ada Leverson's Little Ottleys series. Its motto comes from Shakespeare: love flies when pursued. The story opens at breakfast in a tiny new Knightsbridge flat. Bruce Ottley begs his wife Edith not to make him late for the office.

Edith is young, pretty, and more subtle than she looks. The flat, exactly like thousands of others, frames their married life. Leverson builds comedy from talk, visits, and small social storms. Hyacinth and other friends draw the young couple into wider circles. The novel is light, sharp, and quietly sad about love. It sets up the Ottley books that follow.
my-lady-ludlow:
Elizabeth Gaskell tells this tale through an old woman's memories. The narrator contrasts slow coach days with fast new trains. Letters once came three times a week, and were read like books. Now short, jerky notes fly in twice a day.

Her father was a poor clergyman with a large family. Her mother kept rank with rich makers by wearing old lace. Lady Ludlow rules the world the narrator recalls. V1 dates the novella to 1858 and links it to Cranford. Gaskell draws the old Tory lady with love and irony, as her world of rank gives way to a new, rougher age.
nasa-tm-19650014499-an-exploratory-inves:
William J Alford Jr and William P Henderson ran low-speed tunnel studies on four aircraft shapes with wings that change sweep. Swing wings fly with wings out for slow flight, then swept back for speed. At low speed, that freedom can hurt stability. The fourth shape was designed using lessons from the first three.

That final shape proved steady in pitch for all sweep angles above twelve and a half degrees. It was also steady in direction across the angles and lift levels tested. Its largest static margin was only about nine and a half percent. The study shows design learning in action, shape by shape.
nasa-tm-19660017786-wave-plan-analysis-o:
Don J Wood, Robert G Dorsch, and Charlene Lightner at Lewis Research Center presented a method for computing unsteady flow in liquid-filled systems, in a paper dated July 12, 1965. Unsteady flow surges and settles rather than running evenly. Their wave-plan method builds the flow from small pressure pulses added together. The model runs on a digital computer and covers the whole system at once.

Viscous resistance and other nonlinear effects are included, the summary says. The analysis fits many kinds of hydraulic systems. A long, straight line serves as their worked example. Sudden surges can burst pipes and valves, so a sound prediction method had value far beyond space work.
nasa-tm-19680010756-optimized-computatio:
R. H. Estes and E. R. Lancaster, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, speed up a classic computing method in March 1968. They apply power series integration to the restricted three-body problem. Their new recursion formulas for the series terms cut computing time sharply compared with earlier authors' versions.

The paper also takes up step size: how far the calculation can leap at once. It discusses and extends Van Flandern's method for getting the most step per unit of computer time. Error control guides the choices throughout. A method for keeping the series terms from ballooning is presented as well.
nasa-tm-19700009885-experimental-perform:
David B. Fenn, James N. Deyo, Thomas J. Miller, and Richard W. Vernon ran this test at the Lewis Research Center. Their report came out in January 1970. It covers a Brayton power system, sized from two to fifteen kilowatts, run inside the Space Power Facility.

The engine ran for over five hundred hours in a vacuum, using krypton gas. It was the first run of the complete system, the authors state. Most parts were flight-type hardware, apart from the heat source and heat sink. The report gives the power the engine made and the efficiency it reached at set turbine temperatures and pressures.
nasa-tm-19700014599-interface-stability-:
Eugene P. Symons of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in April 1970. It studies what happens when liquid flows into an empty tank in weightlessness. The tanks tested were cylinders with rounded, bowl-shaped ends, at first holding no liquid at all.

In orbit, liquid does not settle to the bottom of a tank the way it does on Earth. Symons ran tests in a weightless setting to watch the liquid surface, called the interface. He recorded when the inflow stayed stable and when it broke up. Tank designers needed such results to move fuel safely between tanks in space.
people-you-know:
George Ade's People You Know appeared in 1904, illustrated by John T. McCutcheon and others. In his preface Ade warns that the book contains no new information. It holds plain observations about people who live just around the corner, and only those people, so no reader need take painful offence.

He also confesses a shameless amount of slang, since the fables are written in the colloquial American language seldom seen in print. Titles like The Periodical Souse and What Father Bumped Into at the Culture Factory give the flavour. Ade's fables made him America's favourite humorist of everyday vanity.
podcast-joerogan-L6IonRH1-ow:
Commentator Blaire White tells Rogan about her DMT experience in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. White, known for blunt online commentary, here tells a personal story instead of arguing a position. The drug's short, intense trip is the whole subject.

She describes what she saw and felt, and how the minutes under the drug stayed with her afterward. Rogan, who has chased the same experience, compares notes and asks what she made of the beings users report. The segment is a candid trip report from an unlikely reporter, told straight, with the fear and the wonder both left in.
reminiscences-of-captain-gronow: Captain Gronow's Reminiscences recall the high life of Regency England. The guardsman personally knew Wellington, Byron, and Beau Brummell. Bright and amusing anecdotes sparkle on every single page. A firsthand glimpse of a glittering and vanished age.
stories-in-light-and-shadow: Bret Harte's stories in light and shadow: California tales of contrast and character. Varied and vivid, they show his mature art. The West in all its hues. Harte's contrasts are as sharp as sunlight and shadow.
the-autobiography-of-a-quack-and-the-cas: Two Civil War-era medical tales by S. Weir Mitchell, the famous Philadelphia nerve doctor. The first is a rogue's cheerful confession of quackery; the second follows a soldier who loses all four limbs and struggles with phantom pain, a condition Mitchell himself studied. Blending fiction with real medicine, they are landmarks of early American psychological writing.
the-case-of-the-pocket-diary-found-in-th: Auguste Groner's Joe Muller investigates a pocket diary found in the snow, and the secrets frozen in its pages. Patient detection and Viennese atmosphere carry this compact mystery. A gem of early European detective fiction.

what-to-do-thoughts-evoked-by-the-census: Leo Tolstoy wrote What to Do after taking part in the Moscow census of 1882. He saw the city's poor up close and asked why riches and want live side by side. The essay burns with moral force and plain questions. A powerful call to conscience.
